common_name: Elvira Gladiolus (Heirloom Dutch Small-Flowered Pink Gladiolus)

planting.note: Nanus-type corms can go in slightly earlier than large-flowered glads since the hybrid group tolerates cooler soil.

directions: Introduced from Holland in 1956, 'Elvira' belongs to the dainty nanus (primulinus-type) group bred for informal garden display rather than the stiff exhibition spikes of large-flowered glads. Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in well-drained soil; the wiry, lax stems hold loosely spaced soft-pink florets splashed ruby on the lower petals, lending themselves to relaxed cut-flower arrangements rather than staked show spikes. Nanus types are generally hardier and earlier-blooming than grandiflorus gladiolus, so corms can be lifted later in fall or, in milder zones, left mulched in place.

common_name: Starface Gladiolus (Heirloom American Apricot-and-Yellow Patterned Gladiolus)
directions: Raised in Maine and introduced in 1960, 'Starface' is a small-flowered gladiolus prized for intricate Victorian-style patterning rather than solid color, with dappled apricot upper petals over pale-yellow lower petals spiked in ruby. Set corms 4 inches deep after soil has warmed, in full sun with sharp drainage, and stake taller spikes in exposed sites since the slender stems can lean under the weight of bloom. Because this heirloom is a cold-sensitive American seedling rather than a Dutch forcing type, lift and store corms over winter everywhere but the mildest zones.
